items.text: Oops! It looks like you just fell for a phishing attack. Don't worry, this wasn't a real phishing attack. It was a simulated attack run by your organization as part of a security awareness training exercise. So what even is phishing? It's a kind of online scam. You get contacted by a person or company, often through email about something important. You're asked to click on a link or download an attachment. You're then asked to hand over sensitive information such as your email address and password or ask to execute a file. The problem with phishing attacks is they're extremely effective. Did you know that 90% of security breaches are the result of a phishing email? You're probably wondering why. First of all, we as humans love to click and discover. The internet was made for discovering things. So we see a link and our first instinct is to click it. Second of all, our brain loves to infer information and predict things. We see typos and our brain seamlessly fills in the gap. Attackers abuse this by using look-alike email addresses and website domains. Third and finally, urgency. Fishing attacks are designed to put a time pressure on us to act fast. This can cause us to skip much

of the critical thinking we normally apply when browsing the internet. The end result is that phishing attacks are highly successful. So you're probably thinking, what can I do to spot a fish in the future? Fortunately, there's a few common traits to look for. Phishing emails are often unexpected, asking you to bypass a standard procedure or trying to trigger an emotion. If you receive an email with any of these traits, stop. Look at it again and with an extra level of rigor. Do an external validation. Type the sender's email address or domain name into Google. Check to see if any of your colleagues recognize the sender. Look for abnormal typos, more grammatical errors, but if in doubt, report the email to your IT team for further analysis. With this knowledge, you're now equipped to spot the fish.
